prompt: News organisations sometimes publish stories that later turn out to be false. Some people believe that the law should require corrections to be given the same prominence as the original story. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
A false story and its correction are almost never read by the same people. That is the whole of the problem, and it is why leaving the size of a correction to the organisation that got it wrong has never worked. I agree that the law should require corrections to carry the prominence of the original, but prominence was only ever a proxy for something harder to legislate, and a law that fails to say so will not achieve anything.

What matters is not where a correction sits but how many of the people misled by the original ever see it. In print those were roughly the same thing: the front page reached the readership, so a front-page correction reached it again. Online they have come apart. A story can be read a million times through a search result or a shared link and then quietly amended, so that the corrected version is the only one a new reader will ever find while the million who read the false one are never told. A rule written for newsprint would be satisfied by that, and satisfied wrongly.

Drafting it properly means accepting two things publishers dislike. The correction has to be pushed to the audience that received the original, through the same alert, the same feed, the same subscribers, rather than posted somewhere that audience has no reason to look. And the threshold has to turn on harm rather than on error, because a newsroom required to give equal weight to every misspelt name will treat the rule as noise, and rules treated as noise are not obeyed.

None of this is hostile to journalism. A publication known for correcting itself loudly is more believable, not less, and the outlets that resist the idea most strongly tend to be the ones whose errors are least accidental. The obligation should fall where the damage fell: as visibly as the story, to the people who read it.
title: Making corrections as prominent as the story
